utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Registrar. This is Thursday, and I welcome all representatives of the OTP, our witness. I also welcome Mr. Seselj's associates and Mr. Seselj, as well as everyone helping us in this courtroom. We are in Courtroom II, whereas we were scheduled for Courtroom I, but it seems there is a technical problem and this is why we are sitting a bit late, starting a bit late, because of this technical problem, the nature of which I know nothing. We have a witness who has been granted protection measures. I would like to ask confirmation from Ms. Biersay. Are there protection measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there are both voice -- there's voice distortion as well as face distortion and the grant of a pseudonym for the duration of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to private session, then, for the witness to take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Witness 1062, can you tell the Chamber the significance of April 4th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 4th of April was our holiday, Bajram, and I had many guests, more of them Serbs than Muslims, because we socialised more with Serbs. We somehow trusted them more, and my husband and my children and I had more friends against -- amongst Serbs than our own people. However, we could not believe at that time what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court, what kind of holiday is April 4th? Is it a religious holiday or some other kind of holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a religious holiday, an important holiday in our religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What religion is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The events that you just generally described for the Court, occurring on April 4th, do you remember of what year that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just so I understand, on April 4th of 1992, you were celebrating that holiday you just described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this celebration, there are both Serbs and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were both, but there were more Serbs than our own people, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the Serb friends that you had, whether or not they left that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They sat there a while, had drinks, and at -- but nobody gave us an inkling of what they were going to do, or they didn't say, "Look, friend, take care of your children, put them somewhere safe, the Muslims would be attacked ." None of them would say a word so that we could at least save our children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, these Serbian friends, who were more numerous than the Muslims during this party, left, but did they know that there was going to be an attack? Because they left, but did they know? How did they know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they probably knew. In all likelihood, they knew, because they sat there for a while and then they moved out, they moved away. We were asking them, "Tell us, neighbour, where are you going?" And they would say, "We're going off to our weekend cottage." And it was strange to us, how come everybody was suddenly going away for the weekend. And there was even a family who did not have a weekend cottage, but they, too, were going away for the weekend. That's the kind of friends they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Madam Witness, that there were announcements about what residents were supposed to do, as far as going into shelters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the 5th and the 6th that the radio announced that we should not go out into the street, that we should go down into shelters, that we should hide, that we should not walk in the street, and that's what we did. We took cover in shelters, and even in the shelters where we hid, many more people died than out in the street, because the whole building, with 22 occupants in it, they all went down into the shelter and they were all killed. Twelve men from my building alone were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just so that I understand, you started going down into the shelter the day after this holiday on April 4th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The holiday was a Saturday. There was a rally outside the assembly on Sunday, and they were saying there would be no war so we shouldn't be afraid, there would be no war at all, but still, just in case, we should go down to the basement or shelters, if there was a shelter. So the 4th was Bajram, and on the 5th they started these announcements that we should go down into our basements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Was there a shelter in your building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, those who were telling you to go to the basement or these shelters, were they Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was on the radio, it was an announcement on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But radio, which radio? Radio Belgrade or Radio Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radio Zvornik, because Zvornik had its own radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who controlled Zvornik Radio? Was it the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time before the war, it was independent, it was an independent radio station.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How often would -- well, let me back up. The shelter, was there a shelter in your building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe it for the members of the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to describe it, all of it? The shelter was a large -- rather large room, and we took cover there, children, women, men. There were 12 grown men among us, there were 2 infants, 3 or 4 children of various ages, and there were about 15 or 16 of us women. And suddenly --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How often would you go into the shelter? Were you there all day every day or just certain times of day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would be there not so long during the day. We would go home to cook some food and then go back down into the shelter. But we spent all night in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The number of people that you just described, are those people who all lived in your building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, there were two men and two younger men from the adjacent buildings. In fact, one man and two youths from the neighbouring house. Fahrudin and Ekrem took shelter with us, and Senad.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you know all of these people who were with you in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew them all, because we had lived next-door to each other all that time. Those were buildings next-door to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not they were Serbs or non-Serbs, the other people in the shelter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were all Muslims. Only one among us was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court the event involving the blowing up of the door to the shelter? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. On the 9th, it was, the morning of the 9th, around 9.30, 10.00 a.m. It was quiet inside, and then suddenly there was such a large explosion, we were all is shattered. And as this explosion happened, the door to the shelter was suddenly opened, and then masked people, Arkan's men, came in. They rounded up the men right away. They lined them up outside against the wall, and then they came in and they introduced themselves. They said, "We are Seselj's men. We came to defend you, whereas Arkan's men are killing you." So they rounded up the rest of us, the women and the smaller children.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's take it bit by bit. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When the door was blown open, the people who came in, do you remember approximately how many of them came into the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a few, certainly no less than seven or eight. They stood there in the doorway and led out our people from the shelter one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "they let out our people one by one," were they just -- did they lead out the men and women or just the men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the men. Only the men were led out and taken away. And once the men had been taken away, these men came in and introduced themselves. They said, "We are Seselj's men. We came here to save you, to rescue you."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The men who came in later and said they were Seselj's men, were those the same people who had taken the men out first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. One set had green suits of all colours and Arkan's men had black camouflage uniforms or masked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The men with the masks, are they the ones who led the men out of the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you described them as Arkan's men; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How do you know they were Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, because I watched them on television, a programme in which Arkan was training his men, and they were wearing the same uniforms that we saw them in. I watched that more than once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the men in your group were led outside, the people calling themselves Seselj's men came in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were they wearing masks as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After they told you that they were there to save you, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they led us out. They said we had to leave, and they took us to a library room, a sort of community hall for elderly people, where they would play chess and drink tea. We called it the reading room.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How far away was this reading room from your apartment where the shelter was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifty metres perhaps, one hundred metres, not more. It was close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the point at which you and the group -- other group, and the group of women are being led out of the shelter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did these -- did these same men lead you and the women and children out of the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those men who burst into the shelter, rounded us up, and took us into the reading room, and then they went back out and continued to round up other neighbours. Only one of them stayed to guard us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were being taken out of the shelter, where were you in the group of people who were being taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the last to come out, and I was about to turn around to look at my children and my neighbours when one of them prodded me with his automatic rifle in the shoulder blade and told me I must not turn around. And as soon as we got out into the road, those men started shooting, and it was clear to us that they were shooting at our people, because they were not shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: There appears to be a problem with my mic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam, let's take it bit by bit. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The person who put the automatic rifle between your shoulder blades, was that person with the Seselj's men's group or with the Arkan's men's group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you described the shooting that you heard, who was doing that shooting? Was the shooting -- did you see the Seselj's men shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arkan's men were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you see Arkan's men shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see them shooting. I only -- because they wouldn't let us turn around, I told you. I was about to turn around when that fellow stopped me by prodding me in the back with his rifle, but the others who were up the street, children and women, who were being led away, they were 12. They all saw those dead people, and they couldn't have been mistaken. There were 12 of them. They saw the same thing. These men were going from house to house, from door to door, killing men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described -- when you were being led out of the shelter, you described that you wanted to turn around to look at your children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At any point when you came out of the shelter, did you see the men who had been in the shelter with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them lined up against the wall, but the only one I saw was Ivo Kojic, the Croat neighbour from our building. He was the only one that I was able to see before this man prodded me with his rifle. And when we were going out onto the road from the area in front of the building, they started shooting. And I tried to turn around again, and this man hit me very hard. I had a bruise for a long time from that blow with the rifle, the automatic rifle, because I was the last in the group, I was in the back of the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long did it take you to go from your apartment building to the reading room that you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The place where this reading room is, were there other official-type buildings nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was across from the municipal building, across the road from the municipal building. And in that same yard, there was a general goods store, and these Seselj's men, the ones who were ostensibly good guys, were pretending to be good guys.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did they do, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shattering the shop windows of that general goods store, taking out things, chocolate bars to give to the children. They took cigarettes to give to us women, but we women refused to take anything from them. The children, however, took chocolate bars from them. And they were like good guys, allegedly guarding us, protecting us from Arkan's men, looting that store to give us things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went to that reading room, was there anybody else already there or was your group the first group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were the first to get there. Afterwards, they brought others. They went down the street. They killed all the men they found inside the houses, and they brought the women and children to where we were. The children were screaming, crying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You said that the men were guarding you. Are we still talking about Seselj's men? Are they the ones who were guarding you and your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this man himself said he was Seselj's man, and the ones in the basement also introduced themselves as Seselj's men. The one in the reading room said, "We are Seselj's men. We are guarding you, whereas Arkan's men are killing you." Afterwards, a man came with his pockets full of syringes. We were frightened because we didn't know whether it was poison or drugs, and we were even more frightened. He took the syringes out of his pockets, put them on the table in front of the one who was allegedly guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The person who brought these syringes, was this person wearing a military-type uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a green military-type uniform, a camouflage uniform. It was Seselj's colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many Seselj's men were guarding you and the women and children in that reading room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One at that time, but they came and went. One was sitting there all the time next to the door, guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did this Seselj's men have any type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had weapons. All of them had automatic rifles or submachine-guns and pistols. I didn't even know what an automatic was until I saw one. I didn't know what it was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At any point, were any of the women in your group allowed to leave the library or the reading room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Vera Leskovac was there. Seselj might know her. And she recognised a young man and she said to him, "Child, I know you from somewhere." And he said to her, "I know you, too, because you have a daughter in Belgrade." And she said, "Yes, I do." She said where she lived, and this young man said, "I know her very well." And she asked to go home and change.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The young man to whom she was speaking, was he wearing any type of military outfit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She asked him where he was from, and he said he was from Loznica. Well, he said, "Of Loznica." He didn't really say what place exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So this person you just described, this woman, she was allowed to leave the reading room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she was allowed to leave, to go home and change take some more clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did she go by herself or was she escorted by someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was escorted by a woman in uniform. This woman was also wearing a green camouflage uniform. And then Granny Sadeta asked the same thing and they let her go, too. They were the only two allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did they return to the reading room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This woman who was wearing a uniform took them to their home to get changed, and then they came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did these women who came back say about what they had seen outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't dare say that at the time, but later on, when we were released, Vera said to a neighbour, Zuhara, in Banja Koviljaca, she said that she soiled her pants when she saw all our neighbours lying there dead. She didn't dare say anything in front of them. They wouldn't let us talk among ourselves, only if they asked a question, and they didn't ask us, they asked the children. They would ask the children where our people with the rifles were, where our neighbours were. Well, nobody had weapons. Had they had weapons, they wouldn't have been sitting in the shelter. They questioned the children, not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An essential issue, Witness. Those men who were together with you in the shelter, did they have any weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't have even a pocket knife, let alone weapons. Had they had weapons, they wouldn't have been in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question: The men who were together with you in the shelter, did they belong to the TO or did they have a military status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, none of them did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Witness, at any point while you were in the library, the reading room, did anyone tell you what was going to happen to you next? What did they tell you, and who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't tell us anything, but Arkan came in and said to this Seselj's man that a bus would come to collect us and take us on. Some 10 minutes later, the bus did come, and they put us inside, and we went as far as the bridge in Karakaj. There, Arkan got off the bus, and the driver asked, "What are you going to do with them?" We thought they were going to kill us and throw us into the River Drina. That's what we thought. But he said we should go and they should let us go wherever we wanted, we would drop dead on our own, they didn't need to kill us. However, thank God some of us have survived to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about the people on the bus. When your group got on the bus, were there already people on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just us from the reading room, the driver, and Arkan. They got us onto the bus and drove us off, and then they let us get off the bus in Banja Koviljaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there also men on the bus, other men, not Arkan or the driver, but other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Arkan got off before the bridge, before we set out across the bridge towards Banja Koviljaca. He got off, but there were other men from other buildings, not from my buildings. Not a single man from my building survived, but there were some from other buildings. Some Serbs helped them and brought them there. I don't know what happened to them later on, because we got off the bus at Banja Koviljaca and then we all went our different ways, finding our way as best we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were on the bus, did you see anyone being removed from the bus before you got off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we crossed the bridge, yes, there was a dentist. His name eludes me now. I can't recall at present what his name was, and two others. I know one was a dentist or dental technician. They took him off the bus. I can't recall his name now. I was fortunate to remember what my own name was, I was so depressed. Someone who hasn't experienced this can't understand what it was like. That's all I can say. Anyone who hasn't been through this can't believe what it was like. And they talk about reconciliation. What sort of reconciliation? Never. There can be no forgiveness and no reconciliation, ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The place where you finally got off the bus, where was that? Was that in Bosnia or in another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was in Serbia. Banja Koviljaca is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Witness, did there come a time when you returned to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven or eight days later, I came back to check where my family were. I wanted at least to see their bodies, but I couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who did you first go to when you were trying to find the bodies of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, they sent us to Dragan Nikolic. He was like some sort of general. First I went to see him. There were guards there. It was in a commercial enterprise, where they were quartered, and the guard went to fetch him. And he came and brought two books with him. One of them contained the names of those who had been killed and the other of those who had been taken prisoner, and he said they weren't on either of the lists, either those killed or taken prisoners, so he said, "They escaped, they ran away." And I said, "Well, how could they have?" There were so many Seselj's men and Arkan's men, how could they run away? And then we went to see Grujic, the president of the municipality. He said, "Go home and take a look. See if they've taken shelter somewhere, but don't go on your own, find someone to go with you." And then a man named Bato came along. He used to socialise with my children a little. He wasn't a regular friend, but they did socialise, and he came along. And the president said to him, "Bato will take you," and Bato took us home. But Dragan sent a truck, this Dragan Nikolic, he sent a truck, and he said, "You can get on the truck with them." But we didn't trust them, we didn't want to get on the truck with them, so we said, "No, no, we'll go on foot." And it's three kilometres between Karakaj and Zvornik. We went on foot and we came to Grujic, and Grujic said we had to find someone and then this Bato came along, and Bato took us along to our building. And when we got to this building, this truck that Nikola [as interpreted] had been sent was parked in front of the building. And there was a man standing on the steps of the building, and he had an automatic rifle pointing, and he said to us, "See how you're lying." There was a pile of rifles there. They said, "See how you're lying. This is what we found, all those guns." Well, I don't know, maybe they put them there. He said, "Look what we found with them." And I said, "No, no, nobody in Zvornik ever had that. We've never seen those guns before, those rifles." And he said, "Do you want to go with them?" And I said, "All right, kill me. Here I am, kill me." And then this Bato challenged him, and he said, "Get away from here," and he said, "Grujic sent me." I had some gold jewellery, I had some money because my husband had had a good job and a good salary, and I said, "Well, let me take this money so I have something to live on," to take this from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What happened after Bato intervened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He let us go, and we went to our apartments, and they switched on the engine of the truck and left. Bato went to the building with us. We went through the rooms, but we found nothing. Everything had been taken away. There was nothing left there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you go to the spot where you had last seen your -- one of your neighbours outside after you had been taken from the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had been lined up against the wall underneath my balcony. That's where they were killed. There were lots of bullet holes there. My husband's cap was there, one of my son's trainers, and there was blood all over. Twelve men, all of them youngish. There was so much blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you visited the place you just described, did you stay in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No one could stay. They'd killed everyone. When someone goes from Bijeljina or Tuzla, they took people off buses and killed them. They tricked us. They said we should come and report by the 15th of May, that we should register our houses, our apartments. And on that occasion, they killed a lot of people, when they tricked us by saying we should come and register our property.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Witness, when you were being taken from your apartment building to the reading room, did you see any dead bodies at all on that journey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw Hakija Sehic, he was a tailor. I saw Izet, a veterinary surgeon. That was on the road from my house. And then when we were on the bus, I saw a man, a woman, and their son, but somebody saved the son. He was lying there wounded, but he wasn't dead. The father of that boy and his mother were dead. And then on our way to Karakaj, every three or four metres, there was someone lying there dead. Some bodies had been covered, some not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would request that we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session. Witness, would you like us to have a break now or can you still stay seated for a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can, fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that would conclude the questions from the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have just one brief question, and then we can have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you were in the shelter -- were you in the shelter because of shelling? Why did you go down into the shelter after the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had been warned not to walk around the street, that we should go into the basement or shelters in order not to be hit by accident, because there was shooting from Mali Zvornik, and between us and Mali Zvornik there was only the Drina River. So we did take cover there in order not to be shot by accident. However, we were not shot by accident. They simply burst in and killed off everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from -- there was shooting from Mali Zvornik in the direction of Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zvornik itself, right. It was on the 7th and the 8th, when there was -- shot around a little bit to scare people. But on the 9th, they really came into Zvornik and started the killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I will now address the crucial issue, but we have understood, according to your testimony, that your husband and your two sons were killed and the bodies were never found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were never found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single one of them. Now, what we are interested in is this, Witness: Who did what. You us that there were Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you described to us how they were dressed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Himself in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you saw these with your own eyes. Now, we are interested in Seselj's men, Seselj's group. This group of Seselj's men, how many were they all in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite a few. We were not able to count them, but there were lots of them. They were not even walking around. They were like beasts marching around, not like human beings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many were they; 10, 20, 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not 100, but every two or three metres, two or three of them were standing, and there were women among them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were also girls in this group, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that they wore all kinds of clothing. Were there any distinctive features that you could distinguish? Were some wearing headgear or insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... had this Seselj's emblem. You know that, four S, the four S letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What were these insignia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These four Ss, had you seen them before, had you seen those insignia before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Until then, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time you saw them was when you were captured or when they were going down the street? These insignia were on which part of the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the sleeve here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that these were Seselj's men, you say that because that's what they claimed they were, or were these Arkan's men saying that these were Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore different uniforms than Arkan's men. Arkan's men took Zvornik in three or four days and they moved on, and then these ones came, but that's how it went. First Arkan's men came to capture a town, and then they were followed by this other group, who finished it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are interested in the second group, Seselj's men. You say they were Seselj's men. Is that because you heard it after the war, or did you hear that in Zvornik on April 9, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 9th of April, all of them introduced themselves as Seselj's men, and they swore by Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their accent, was it a local accent or did it sound like a Serbian accent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their speech was different from the local Serbs. Local Serbs do not draw out their syllables. They speak clearly. In Serbia, they speak differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this group, so-called "Seselj's men," were there some of your own Serbs, local Serbs that were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't make it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And there's a third group that does not appear, but I believe I must ask a question about them. Were there JNA soldiers also? Did you see any, or did you only see Arkan's men and Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. We women were frightened out of our socks. We could not look around. We were not able to pay too much attention and say that somebody was JNA or Seselj's men. We reacted mostly to the Serbian dialect from Serbia proper. But later, when I came back to Zvornik to check out my apartment and to register it, then I realised there were our local Serbs among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, Witness. We'll now have a 20-minute break. That way you can rest, and we will resume in 20 minutes, and I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before Mr. Seselj starts his cross-examination, the interpreters told me that there was a slight problem, because in putting the questions, the witness tends to answer extremely quickly and there's overlapping, and it's very difficult to interpret. So I'm asking all parties to please make a break between questions and answers. Mr. Seselj, we're now in open session. If you want to raise questions that might identify the witness, we will move into private session, but you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Madam, I'm really sorry about the tragedy of your life, and I would much rather not ask you anything. However, I still have to clarify something with you. You used to live, as I understood, in the very center of the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on the 8th of April there was fighting in Zvornik, and that was the reason why you and your family and your neighbours took cover in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, not the 8th, but the 9th, the 9th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 9th, your door was flung open by explosives, but before that there was fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Zvornik. There was shooting from Mali Zvornik. There was nothing in Zvornik, itself. In Zvornik, there was shooting on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. The date doesn't matter. Maybe you don't even remember precisely. I have here the statement that you gave to the Security Information Service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember when the officers of that police service talked to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was on the 4th -- in fact, the 3rd of February, 2003, in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You remember now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you that statement, so could the usher please take this document, 0341-9107 and put it on the ELMO, but showing only the document on the ELMO that is visible in the courtroom. It shouldn't go out into the public so we don't have to go into closed session. Do you have that document in your electronic system? I adjusted to your electronic courtroom more easily than your own court management, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: May I -- can I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you remember that talk with them. Tell me, how many officers were talking to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I never talked to any of our own officers. I talked to people from The Hague, the services of The Hague in Sarajevo. Twice, I think, that was all. I didn't talk to our authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I have a document from which it is obvious that you did talk to the agents of the Intelligence and Security Service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please show the lady the document so that she can see the signature on both pages, on the bottom of page 1 and then on the second page as well. Could you please put it on the ELMO. I still don't see it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this your signature on the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it then a forgery of your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, but my signature is different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, since I don't have the original signature of that -- of the lady, I would like to see the real signature of the witness. I suppose she must have provided one for your documentation, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here the original signature, when the witness signed the document under seal, and it could look alike. We will show it to the Prosecution and to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, Madam, that it's the same signature on the document of the Intelligence and Security Service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's the same to the signature that you gave for the record to the ICTY. It could be a forgery, but I'm not the one who would forge your signature, because this document was given to me by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution got it from the Intelligence and Security Service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the stamp of that service is on the document. So you claim this is not your signature and you never spoke to that service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's interesting to me is that you gave a statement here in which you described the details of the events whose victim you were, the events in which your husband and your two sons were killed, but in this document you never mentioned Seselj's men. That's why this document is important to me. However, since you claim that you never spoke to that service, I would like the Trial Chamber to acquaint itself with this document of the Intelligence Security Service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and since you claim this is not your signature, that your signature was forged, I have no further questions, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I do not wish to add anything to the very painful experience you went through, and everyone here in this courtroom has fully understood your ordeal. However, the accused is entitled to challenge what any witness has said. The accused received from the Prosecution a great number of documents, and this document, which bears an official stamp -- well, I don't have the translation into English, but with the stamp I can note that it was drawn up on February 4th, 2003. This document bears your name, your date of birth. You are a protected witness, so I will not give either your name or your date of birth, but in this document there is a description of the events that occurred. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a slight correction. The date on the last page of the document is the 3rd of February, 2004, and it might assist the witness if she's reminded that it's a statement that she gave to authorities in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must intervene. I did remind the witness that it's a statement given in Tuzla, and she denied it. I don't think we should force the witness, who is in a very bad state of mind and very bad physical condition, to recall something. I don't think it would be humane. She probably does not believe my sincere sympathy, and I can justify even her hatred towards me, and I can find justification for any hatred that results from such a tragedy. But I don't think that what the Prosecutor did in examination-in-chief would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, let me finish. Witness, on February 3rd, 2003, we have a document which seems to bear your signature. This document, dated February 3rd, 2004 [as interpreted], also bears an official stamp dated February 4th, 2003, so it seems that the document -- it took at least a month for this document to reach a central organisation that recorded it. You said you never went to Tuzla. Are you absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that to the authorities in Tuzla or to the authorities anywhere in our country, I never said anything about this. It's only that in Tuzla, they called me and came to fetch me in the car. But it was your own officers. If I could see that woman now, I could recognise her. I talked to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. I'm trying to shed light on this. You were saying that people from this Tribunal came to get you in a car. These people from the Tribunal, were they speaking English, were they speaking your own language? How many were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They spoke English, they spoke English, and the driver was our local man from Bosnia. He took my passport to make a copy, and it was said that I should come next year, the following year, but I didn't come until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you can understand English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This person speaking English, how could she convey -- how could she convey what she wanted to say? Who was the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an interpreter. There were two of them, one man, one woman. And in addition to them, there was one person from Bosnia who interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the car there were four people; yourself, the lady from the Tribunal, the interpreter, and the driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where did you go, all four of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in an office in Tuzla. It's towards -- it was an institutional building on the way to Gradina, in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This office in Tuzla, was it an office of the Tuzla police? What office was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whose office it was, but we were not there long. A few months after that conversation, the same driver came to fetch me, took me somewhere to have my blood samples taken. He went to my apartment to take my passport to make a copy. He said he would find a Xerox machine to have that copy ready to avoid delays like the first time. But I never went to our authorities, and I never explained anything to our authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were in Tuzla. Did they ask you to sign a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed them and we talked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one that I just saw? It's not that one -- it's not that document, because that's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You signed a document, but not this one, because you're saying this is not your signature. But the document you signed, was it written in your own language or was it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- I signed in my language, if I signed, when I gave a statement to those people who introduced themselves and showed their official IDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What year was this? What year did you go to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2004, because in 2003 I was here, I went here, not to Tuzla. In Tuzla -- they took me to Tuzla later, after I had been here, and I was here in 2003, on the 1st of September, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our problem is the following, Witness: We have this document bearing a signature. You're saying this is not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document looks very much like an official document. I don't understand your language, but I get the impression that it is very similar to the statement you made to the OTP, except for one crucial element. In this document, there is no mention of any presence of Seselj's men. Seselj's men appear with the documents from the OTP, which is why we have a problem. The question is very straightforward. From the very onset to the -- the very first people to ask you questions about what had happened to your family and to yourself, from the onset did you say that it was Arkan's men and Seselj's men, or did you say nothing regarding the identification of those who perpetrated these crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said the same story like today, because I cannot forget my pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you recollect, Witness, and we all understand that such an event will stay etched into your memory forever, but as far as you recollect, can you tell us when you were able to relate everything that had happened to a third party, a person investigating, either authorities from your own country or investigators from the OTP? Could you tell us, as far as you recollect, in what year you started relating all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave my first statement in Berlin. At that time, I was in Germany, in Berlin, when I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Could we please move to private session for this portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: And I wanted to correct something. I had asked for the floor much earlier, but you didn't give it to me then. It's maybe a mistake of the interpreter or the translator, but I can't know that until you tell me what it is about. When you spoke about the document given to the Federation services of Bosnia-Herzegovina, once you mentioned the year 2003 and once you mentioned the year 2004. On one page, we see that it was signed on the 3rd of February, 2003, but it was registered in the registry of the service a day later, the 4th of February, 2003. Maybe I should clarify this. Maybe it was not your mistake, but the way I heard it in interpretation, it was not precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are absolutely right. The document here is dated February 3rd, 2003, and the stamp has been -- has the date that is the day after, February 4, 2003. There is no mention of 2004 on this document. Witness, despite all the questions I put to you, you keep telling us that this is not your signature. I will hand this document back to you, and please look at it very carefully. There are two signatures, one on the first page and another one on the second page. There are two signatures. Please check them very carefully, all two of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the witness is looking at this, Mr. President, the Prosecution has a translation of this document into English, and I move that they show it to the Chamber. There is a document in English, but I had to throw away everything that was in English because I didn't have anywhere to store it. So I made a selection and kept the documents in Serbian and either returned the English versions to the OTP or threw them away. So they must have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, normally you have the translation. I don't have it. And with the translation, we would be able to check whether this text corresponds to the document dated 1996. Witness, you looked at the two signatures. You still maintain that these are not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one page, it looks like mine. But this other one, I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On which sheet could it be your signature, the first one or the second one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But this one, I wouldn't say that was mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't make any statements to our authorities, any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The signature is not your signature, or is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is yours. We will now look at the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move back into open session, because the reasons for private session are no longer in existence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the witness is reviewing the statement, perhaps it would help if she reviewed the first paragraph, and I ask for -- to remain in private session only because it mentions an address. So in addition to looking at the signatures, if she could also read the first paragraph, perhaps that would assist her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at the first paragraph of this document, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. Judges, I think it's highly inappropriate to force a witness, who has stated more than once that this document does not bear the witness's signature and that it's not the witness's statement, that the witness is being made to recognise this. I think this is impermissible, and I ask you to stop this sort of pressure on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, everyone is trying to gauge whether what you're saying is true or not. This document confirms your theory, i.e., when this person made her statement, Seselj's men were never mentioned, which this document proves. But on the OTP's document, Seselj's men are mentioned. So if you are telling us the opposite now, very well, but I don't understand. I don't understand what your position is. This person -- this woman said, A, "This is not my signature," and then we discover that in fact there are two signatures, one which she does not challenge, but the other one she does challenge.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain my position in all this, then. I showed the witness a document. She stated that she had never made that statement and that these are not her signatures. Now the witness is being maltreated. It's not my aim to have the witness exposed to pressure here. I presented the evidence I had. I put it to the witness, and that was the end of it. Now you're trying to force the witness to remember something she doesn't remember. Why shouldn't a witness have the right not to remember something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are not going to make much more of this. My colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't give this to our authorities. I could only have given a statement to the Prosecutors from The Hague. I never made any statements to our authorities, nor did anybody ever ask me about it or call me up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move back into open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please allow me. I would like to put my question. Witness, what I wanted to know is this: Your authorities have never investigated in the tragedy you experienced. You were never compensated, if one can use this term, for this tragedy. And you received no pension from the authorities of your country because you lost your husband and your children, the authorities of your country in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I did. First, I reported the missing persons. I was rejected. They were not recognised. I wasn't recognised any compensation for missing person. Then I asked for my husband's pension. I was granted my husband's pension. I had to take out various documents. I did, and I handed them over to get his pension. A year ago, they recognised the missing persons claim, and I began receiving that as well, but not until last year. But nobody from the authorities ever came round to ask how I was, so no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This procedure was launched without you establishing any kind of contact with the authorities who were in charge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I handed over documents for missing persons in order to get something. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Witness. You said at some point in time that the same driver, the one who drove you, you were together with an employee of this Tribunal and an interpreter. The same driver who took you to Tuzla was a man who at some point in time came, if I understood you correctly, came to take a blood sample?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for him to take the blood sample, but they took me where blood samples were being taken for DNA. He didn't take the blood sample. He drove me there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I protest that all of this is going on in private session for no reason. I think this is scandalous. There was no reason for us to move into private session. We've been in private session for half an hour, and there is not a single objective reason for us to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Witness, this driver drove you so that somebody could take this blood sample. So it's the authorities of your country who asked you to do this, so that one could find the bodies of your relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The driver who came to collect me, he took me to this agency, where your agents were, and this driver introduced himself and showed me an ID, and he took me first to your people and we spoke, and then a few days later he came to my house and took me somewhere for me to give a blood sample.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session, the Trial Chamber is confronted with the following problem: During the examination-in-chief of the witness, the Prosecutor put questions to the witness based on material collected in September 1996; to be more specific, on the 24th of September, 1996. During the cross-examination, Mr. Seselj has produced a document coming from the security services of Sarajevo, dated the 3rd of February, 2003. This document is stamped. The stamp indicates what the origin of the document is, and the stamp is dated the 4th of February, 2003. It seems that on this second document, the document of 2003, no mention was made of the presence of Seselj's men. Therefore, the accused has shown us this piece of evidence. Now, if we compare this with the document of 2003, and when the two documents were presented to her, the witness does not recognise her signature. And as I expressly requested her to check this, she checked these signatures. On the document, in B/C/S, there is a signature on the first page and a signature on the second page. The witness was not so positive as far as one of the signatures was concerned, whilst saying that she was never interviewed by the official services of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but that she was only interviewed by the investigators of the OTP. And she stands by this statement of hers. This is how things stand: At the moment, we have still not solved this issue. So, Madam Prosecutor, you would like to put a question to the witness, who met with members of the OTP yesterday, and this was the question which you had put; is that right, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and before I request that we move into private session for the question, I'd like to remind the Chamber that 65 ter number 5017 is the 92 bis package that had been previously submitted for admission under that Rule, and from that document, on the face of it, there was a meeting on the 22nd of February, 2003, for the signing of that 92 bis package. I just wanted to highlight that for the Chamber. And, Your Honours, at this time if we could briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move back into private session, because you would like to mention a fact which could perhaps identify the witness. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move back into private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you would like to take the floor again and put questions to the witness, or do you have no further questions? It's whatever you feel you would like to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed my cross-examination, and I said that loud and clear. Now I just want to present my demand that the previous private session, that lasted about half an hour, be made entirely public, because no address was mentioned there. If there is any reason for this current little private session now to remain private because of the address, I agree, but those -- half an hour, sometime ago I demanded that they be made public, because otherwise my rights in this trial would be considerably violated. Without the public nature of the trial, I have no interest in defending myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your application has been recorded. We will see whether lifting part of the private session is justified. We shall see whether this should remain in private session. It should remain in private session as far as the address is concerned, solely. Ms. Biersay, we have finished, unless you have other questions you would like to put.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to thank you. Would you like to add something? I saw that you raised your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do want to show you the documents that I now recently got from Republika Srpska, and I want to show you that my details are recorded incorrectly. I also have my personal ID card. They changed my name. It's not my real name. I told them I wanted my name recorded properly, and they told me, "You have to go to the Official Gazette and go --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Forgive me. I was anticipating the revelation of some private information, but I don't think we're there yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as the official papers are concerned which raise questions because your name seems to have been changed, well I trust you, and I'm not going to ask you to show us your passport, because there's no direct link here with what we're discussing. This is not relevant, as far as your testimony is concerned, which relates to what happened in 1992. Therefore, I would like to thank you, on behalf of the Judges of this Bench, to have come to testify in The Hague at the request of the Prosecution. And as my fellow Judge has told you, we feel a great deal of sympathy for you and given what you have lived through. Before adjourning, I would like the usher should escort you out of the courtroom. You can leave the courtroom, because the blinds have been dropped and you may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now turn to Mr. Mundis and ask him what the schedule for next week is to be. I put my -- I asked these questions yesterday already, and I wanted to know whether the upcoming witnesses will be a problem or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone. I'm not in possession of any information that would lead me to conclude that there would be any changes to the schedule as previously circulated. VS-007, as far as I know, will be here to testify next week. In the event that situation changes, the Trial Chamber and Dr. Seselj will be notified as soon as such information comes into our possession.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if there are any changes, I have absolutely no capacity, no resources, to prepare for new witnesses. I only have the documents for the witness announced for next week and the witness announced for the week after. All the other documents are still boxed. They're not even in binders, because to save room I took them all out of binders and put them in boxes. And until I get the opportunity to sort out the boxes, I cannot even find the right documents for a witness who hasn't been announced so far. I'm only ready for these two that are scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, this can be admitted. There are two documents for next week and the week after -- two witnesses for next week and the week after that. If the next witness cannot come then please call another witness. Given that the cells are being done up at the moment, the accused would not be able to read these documents, so you might want to plan for a third witness that has not been scheduled so far. I've asked you to prepare a list of the videos that could be shown, Mr. Mundis, in case we were to be without a witness. How do things stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we are, as I indicated yesterday, still undertaking that review. I'm not sure if we have any category A videos left. This team had divided the videos into category A videos and category B videos. I'm not -- as I just said, I'm not sure there are any category A videos remaining. I will get back to you as soon as we're able to make a final determination on that, and I will revisit the issue as soon as we adjourn for today. But I'm not sure we'll be in a position to show any videos. I, again at this point, do not have any reason to believe that the witnesses scheduled for the next two weeks will not be coming, so I think it might be premature to be planning anything in the event those two witnesses don't come. I will say, however, that perhaps -- and this is also something I'll be getting to a little bit later today. I do envision sending a letter to Dr. Seselj concerning the possibility of meetings with respect to any agreed facts. That has come up again on the record just a few weeks ago. So we may be in a position whereby in the event a hearing were to have to be cancelled for any reason, that we might be -- we might be in a position to use that time in order for myself or members of my team and Dr. Seselj to perhaps have a meeting to discuss agreed facts or any other types of stipulations. So that is something else that I will be, as I indicated, sending a letter to Dr. Seselj on in the next day or two. So that might be another way of constructively using time that otherwise would not be available due to the fact that a witness or witnesses might not appear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber can only encourage this, all parties, actually, to meet, so that together you tell the Trial Chamber that you agreed on such-and-such facts, and then you can really work on the points that are challenged, because this would really help save time. As an example, talking about Zvornik, for example, there's no challenge about the fact that events occurred in Zvornik. This could be agreed by both parties. The challenge, of course, is who did what, but this is another problem. If both parties can agree as to the fact that there were events that occurred in Zvornik or elsewhere, then it's not necessary to have witnesses come here in the courtroom to talk about these events, except that of course they could come in order to identify the perpetrators. But at least we could avoid talking about some issues. So it's in everybody's interest for Mr. Seselj to meet with Mr. Mundis -- with Mr. Mundis to meet with Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj said he agreed to that, in order to look into what could be -- what could be subject to a judicial notice that would be then submitted to the Trial Chamber, and then you could redirect yourself towards the elements that are really specific to your cases, and this would really help save a lot of time. For example, the witness who came earlier, we identified extremely well where the problem lied, and there was no need to spend hours on trying to identify this problem. So please meet, you know, and that can only be very profitable, of course, if you meet in the right spirit. You should not meet with a bellicose spirit, but I've known you for a while and I believe that the spirit governing these proceedings is very correct. So please meet as soon as possible, and there might be some positive outcome to this, and the Trial Chamber is ready to save time. This trial has been dragging on for too long. The accused has been waiting for years for this trial. I personally believe, and I've said this on many occasions, that this trial should have been heard earlier and not at this late stage in 2007-2008. Before we adjourn, Mr. Seselj, would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have something to say on this subject, and only on this subject. If you had offered me to meet with the beautiful and charming Ms. Biersay, I may have accepted, but since the offer is to meet with Mr. Mundis, I categorically refuse. For five years, I offered to meet with the Prosecution, in the presence of my legal assistants, and that was my only condition for that meeting, to clarify all facts in dispute, to find what we can stipulate regarding certain historic events. The Prosecution refused this, and they blackmailed me. "Yes, we can, but in the presence of a standby counsel, not your legal assistants." Now, when the trial is ongoing and has been going on for a while, I have no reason anymore to meet with the Prosecutor. I don't want to meet with him. Everything is in dispute now. Even the date today is in dispute. This can be no reason to stop the trial or interrupt it. Maybe you are in a hurry, but I'm no longer in a hurry to get anywhere. I've been here for six years now, and I'm in no hurry any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we've heard you, but I believe that I have to go back in time briefly. Immediately after your initial hearing, you told us that Ms. Carla Del Ponte wanted to meet with you. At the time you accepted, subject to the fact that this meeting be filmed and be carried out in the presence of witnesses, if possible your own witnesses, and Ms. Del Ponte declined, so there was no meeting. At the time when Ms. Dahl took over, took her position, I tried to revive this possible meeting between the two parties. At the time, it seems that you had agreed to it, but for a reason that totally escapes me, Ms. Dahl wasted time and the day she sent you a letter, inviting you for meeting you, you categorically refused to meet with her. A few -- recently, this came back, this whole issue came back, and I thought I understood that you were not really hostile to this kind of meeting, and I believe that it is in this spirit that Mr. Mundis envisaged to send you a letter in order to meet up with you. But now you're saying you no longer want to meet him. I mean, it takes two people to have a meeting, at least. If one is reluctant, what can we do? If you don't want to meet with him, we cannot force you to. However, this is quite regrettable, because, you know, dialogue is always very beneficial. Maybe you disagree with this, and then there will be no meeting and the trial will continue as planned. Out of memory, I say that we gave the Prosecution about 120 or 125 hours to present its case. I think it's 120, not 125. You will be granted the same amount of time to present your own case and your own witnesses, so theoretically, unless we run into a disaster, this trial should end next year in 2009. I cannot add anything to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to add before Mr. Seselj takes the floor. He is not entitled to choose who he is going to meet with from the OTP. The person chosen -- the person from the OTP that he will meet with is chosen by Mr. Mundis. He cannot pick and choose, and he cannot accept or refuse just because he -- supposedly he would meet with a beautiful lady like Ms. Biersay. That is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to clarify two points. If you recall, Mr. President, to the best of my recollection, at the first status conference that you presided over, I think it was in March last year, I reiterated my willingness to have a dialogue with a representative of the OTP under the sole condition that my legal advisers and selected investigators be present. Ms. Dahl hesitated until the end of October. She didn't want that meeting to take place. She took the initiative only a week before the start of trial, and then it was too late. There's another point I have to clarify. I did meet with Ms. Carla Del Ponte. That was after my plea. That was in March 2003, and it wasn't because I said I was willing or asked for a meeting, but because after the status conference and after I entered my plea, the guards forcibly took me to Carla Del Ponte's office. That conversation was rather short. There was an interpreter there and there was her associate. What was her name? Hartman, Florence Hartman was there. The conversation boiled down to mutual compliments. As for the merits, I said I could discuss beletre [phoen] with her or the weather. Anything else I could discuss only in the presence of my legal advisers, and that was the end of our conversation, so the conversations never took place. As for what Judge Lattanzi said, I don't know what your interpretation was, what you heard, but I was making a joke. I assume I have the right to make a joke, to say something humorous from time to time. I didn't say I would choose who was to meet with me from the OTP. I said I might perhaps change my mind or hesitate had I been offered a meeting with the beautiful and charming Ms. Biersay. As you misunderstood my humorous remark, I now withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the first item you mentioned, I fully agree with you. Mr. Mundis, what Mr. Seselj says is true. He had offered for a meeting, as long as he could have his associates with him, which seems logical, and Ms. Dahl, for a reason that I don't know, did not give -- did not follow suit. That's just exactly how it happened, and I'm a witness to this because I was present during the pre-trial -- the status conference, when this was announced. And then later on, a few months later, Ms. Dahl came back on her decision, but Mr. Seselj believed it was too late. I believe that it's never too late in life, but he believed it was too late. That is how things happened. I'd like to thank you all now, and we will meet again on Tuesday in the afternoon, next Tuesday in the afternoon, so at 2.45 next Tuesday, 2.45 because my fellow Judges are sitting in the Delic case. So we resume on Tuesday at 2.45. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of April, 2008, at 2.45 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
[Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.31 a.m.,
